{{Short description|Term in applied mathematics}}
In [[applied mathematics]], the '''Ostrogradsky instability''' is a feature of some solutions of theories having [[equation of motion|equations of motion]] with more than two time [[derivative (mathematics)|derivatives]] (higher-derivative theories).  It is suggested by a theorem of [[Mikhail Ostrogradsky]] in [[classical mechanics]] according to which a non-degenerate [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] dependent on [[time derivative]]s higher than the first corresponds to a [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] [[bounded set|unbounded from below]]. As usual, the Hamiltonian is associated with the Lagrangian via a [[Legendre transformation#Hamilton-Lagrange mechanics|Legendre transform]]. The Ostrogradsky instability has been proposed as an explanation as to why no differential equations of higher order than two appear to describe physical phenomena.<ref>{{Cite journal |title= Third-order equations of motion and the Ostrogradsky instability |journal=Physical Review D|volume=91|issue=8|arxiv=1411.3721|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.91.085009|year=2015|last1=Motohashi|first1=Hayato|last2=Suyama|first2=Teruaki|article-number=085009 |bibcode=2015PhRvD..91h5009M |s2cid=118565011 }}</ref>
However, Ostrogradsky's theorem does not imply that all solutions of higher-derivative theories are unstable as many counterexamples are known.<ref>{{Cite journal |title= On Field theories with nonlocalized action |journal=Physical Review|volume=79|issue=145|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.79.145|year=1950|last1=Pais|first1=A.|last2=Uhlenbeck|first2=G. E.|pages=145–165 |bibcode=1950PhRv...79..145P |s2cid=123644136 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title= On the Problem of Stability for Higher Order Derivatives: Lagrangian Systems |journal= Letters in Mathematical Physics|volume=14|issue=311|doi=10.1007/BF00402140|year=1987|last1=Pagani|first1=E.|last2=Tecchiolli|first2=G.|last3=Zerbini|first3=S.|pages=311–319 |bibcode= 1987LMaPh..14..311P|s2cid=120866609 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title= Benign vs. Malicious ghosts in higher-derivative theories|journal= Nuclear Physics B|volume=706|issue=598|arxiv=hep-th/0407231|doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2004.10.037|year=2005|last1=Smilga|first1=A. ==Outline of proof==
Source:<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Invisible Universe: Dark Matter and Dark Energy |volume=720 |pages=403–433 |arxiv=astro-ph/0601672|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-71013-4_14 |chapter=Avoiding Dark Energy with 1/R Modifications of Gravity |series=Lecture Notes in Physics |isbn=978-3-540-71012-7 |year=2007 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/925754/files/0601672.pdf|last1=Woodard |first1=R.P. |s2cid=16631993 }}</ref>

The main points of the proof can be made clearer by considering a one-dimensional system with a Lagrangian <math>L(q,{\dot q}, {\ddot q})</math>. The [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] is

:<math> \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial{\dot q}}+ \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\frac{\partial L}{\partial{\ddot q}} = 0.</math>

Non-degeneracy of <math>L</math> means that the [[canonical coordinates]] can be expressed in terms of the derivatives of <math>{q}</math> and vice versa. Thus, <math>\partial L/\partial{\ddot q}</math> is a function of <math>{\ddot q}</math> (if it were not, the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] <math>\det[\partial^2 L/(\partial{\ddot q_i}\, \partial{\ddot q}_j)]</math> would vanish, which would mean that <math>L</math> is degenerate), meaning that we can write <math>q^{(4)} = F(q,{\dot q}, {\ddot q}, q^{(3)})</math> or, inverting, <math>q = G(t, q_0, {\dot q}_0, {\ddot q}_0, q^{(3)}_0)</math>. Since the evolution of <math>q</math> depends upon four initial parameters, this means that there are four canonical coordinates. We can write those as

:<math>Q_1 : = q</math>
:<math>Q_2 : = {\dot q}</math>

and by using the definition of the conjugate momentum,

:<math>P_1 : = \frac{\partial L}{\partial{\dot q}} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial{\ddot q}}</math>
:<math>P_2 : =  \frac{\partial L}{\partial{\ddot q}} </math>

The above results can be obtained as follows. First, we rewrite the Lagrangian into "ordinary" form by introducing a Lagrangian multiplier as a new dynamic variable <math>\lambda</math>
:<math>L(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q})\to \tilde{L}=L(Q_1,\dot{Q_1},\dot{Q_2})-\lambda(Q_2-\dot{Q_1})</math>,
from which, the Euler-Lagrangian equations for <math>Q_1,Q_2,\lambda</math> read
:<math>Q_1:\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{Q_1}}+\dot{\lambda}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial Q_1}=0</math>,
:<math>Q_2:\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{Q_2}}+{\lambda}=0</math>,
:<math>\lambda:Q_2-\dot{Q_1}=0</math>,
Now, the canonical momentum <math>P_1,P_2</math> with respect to <math>\tilde{L}</math> are readily shown to be
:<math>P_1=\frac{\partial\tilde{L}}{\partial\dot{Q_1}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q_1}}+\lambda=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q_1}}-\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{Q_2}}</math>
:<math>P_2=\frac{\partial\tilde{L}}{\partial\dot{Q_2}}=\frac{\partial {L}}{\partial\dot{Q_2}}</math>
while
:<math>P_\lambda=0</math>
These are precisely the definitions given above by Ostrogradski.
One may proceed further to evaluate the Hamiltonian
:<math>\tilde{H}=P_1\dot{Q_1}+P_2\dot{Q_2}+p_\lambda\dot{\lambda}-\tilde{L}=P_1Q_2+P_2\dot{Q_2}-{L}</math>,
where one makes use of the above Euler-Lagrangian equations for the second equality.
We note that due to non-degeneracy, we can write <math> {\ddot q}=\dot{Q_2}</math> as <math>a(Q_1, Q_2, P_2)</math>. 
Here, only ''three'' arguments are needed since the Lagrangian itself only has three free parameters. 
Therefore, the last expression only depends on <math>P_1,P_2,Q_1,Q_2</math>, it effectively serves as the Hamiltonian of the ''original'' theory, namely,

:<math>H = P_1 Q_2 + P_2  a(Q_1, Q_2, P_2) - L(Q_1,Q_2,P_2) </math>.

We now notice that the Hamiltonian is linear in <math>P_1</math> and hence unbounded from below. This is a source of the Ostrogradsky instability, and it stems from the fact that the Lagrangian depends on fewer coordinates than there are canonical coordinates (which correspond to the initial parameters needed to specify the problem). The extension to higher dimensional systems is analogous, and the extension to higher derivatives simply means that the phase space is of even higher dimension than the configuration space.
